extracted.intended_audience: educators, philosophers, policymakers, and general readers concerned with free speech, argumentation, and public discourse
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for assessing the quality, vitality, and epistemic adequacy of public argument, debate, and doctrine — including how opinions are formed, defended, and tested in education, religion, and politics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge of the adversary's case
rubrics_metrics.description: He who knows only his own side of the case, knows little of that.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sound opinion requires understanding the reasons on the opposite side as well as one's own. One should study the adversary's case with as great, if not greater, intensity than one's own (example: Cicero). Anti-pattern: relying solely on one's own side and being ignorant of opposing reasons, leading to mere inclination or authority-driven belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation of opposing arguments in their strongest form
rubrics_metrics.description: He must be able to hear them from persons who actually believe them; who defend them in earnest, and do their very utmost for them. He must know them in the most plausible and persuasive form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For genuine understanding, opponents' arguments must be presented and engaged in their most advantageous light, not as straw men or softened versions supplied by one's own teachers. Education should require encountering earnest defenders of contrary views.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that objections be openly stated to be answerable
rubrics_metrics.description: How are objections to be answered if that which requires to be answered is not spoken? Or how can the answer be known to be satisfactory, if the objectors have no opportunity of showing that it is unsatisfactory?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objections must be freely expressed in public debate so they can be properly refuted and evaluated. Anti-pattern: suppressing objections and relying on unseen expert refutations — this leaves no public assurance that objections have been satisfactorily answered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of free publication and access to dissenting writings
rubrics_metrics.description: Everything must be free to be written and published without restraint if the teachers of mankind are to be cognisant of all that they ought to know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restricting access (e.g., permitting only an elite to read heterodox works) undermines the broader intellectual competence of society. Policy or practice that limits publication or readership is an impediment to proper critical engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of negative criticism and dialectic discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative criticism — that which points out weaknesses in theory or errors in practice — is a means to attaining positive knowledge and should be systematically trained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Socratic dialectics and medieval disputations (despite defects) served to force pupils to understand both sides. Modern education's lack of this training reduces the capacity to form real knowledge. Anti-pattern: disparaging negative logic and avoiding critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that cognitive confidence rests on exposure to strongest objections
rubrics_metrics.description: Mankind ought to have a rational assurance that all objections have been satisfactorily answered; philosophers and theologians who are to resolve difficulties must make themselves familiar with those difficulties in their most puzzling form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experts must confront the strongest formulations of objections to confidently assert an answer. Without such exposure, suspension of judgment is the rational stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vitality of doctrines measured by continued debate
rubrics_metrics.description: Not only the grounds of the opinion are forgotten in the absence of discussion, but too often the meaning of the opinion itself. The words which convey it cease to suggest ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When controversy dies away and doctrines become hereditary or received passively, their living power declines. Ongoing dispute and defense keep doctrines meaningful and operative in conduct. Anti-pattern: passive, rote acceptance leading to 'dead beliefs.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Simulation of dissent when unanimity eliminates genuine opponents
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the advantage of explaining and defending truths can no longer be had, teachers should endeavour to provide a substitute: some contrivance for making the difficulties of the question as present to the learner's consciousness as if they were pressed upon him by a dissentient champion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educational practice should recreate the pressure of opposing views (e.g., dialectical exercises) so learners develop real understanding even when genuine dissent is scarce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition that minority opinions often supply omitted truths
rubrics_metrics.description: When conflicting doctrines share the truth between them, the nonconforming opinion is needed to supply the remainder of the truth of which the received doctrine embodies only a part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dissent should be valued because popular opinions are often partial; heretical or unpopular views may contain neglected elements of truth. Anti-pattern: immediate condemnation of minority views as wholly false without assessing their partial contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encouragement and protection of minority/oppositional voices
rubrics_metrics.description: Every opinion which embodies somewhat of the portion of truth which the common opinion omits ought to be considered precious... long as popular truth is one-sided, it is more desirable that unpopular truth should have one-sided assertors too.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political and social health requires both parties (order and reform) to be able to speak and be defended with equal freedom and talent. Policy or practice should encourage and countenance minority opinions rather than suppress them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of reason rather than authority as the ground of premises
rubrics_metrics.description: The school disputations of the Middle Ages had the incurable defect that the premises appealed to were taken from authority, not from reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations of arguments and educational exercises should favor premises grounded in reason and evidence rather than unexamined appeals to authority. Anti-pattern: training that enforces doctrine by authority alone rather than by rational demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness that majority recognition reduces one form of epistemic benefit
rubrics_metrics.description: The loss of so important an aid to the intelligent and living apprehension of a truth, as is afforded by the necessity of explaining it to, or defending it against, opponents... is a drawback from the benefit of its universal recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when unanimity indicates a true opinion, educators and intellectuals should acknowledge and compensate for the lost epistemic advances that come from having to defend against objections (e.g., through contrived challenges or rigorous critique).
